newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-JOPPY AND HOLMES RETAIN MIDDLEWEIGHT TITLES.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-JOPPY AND HOLMES RETAIN MIDDLEWEIGHT TITLES.

text.p: William Joppy and Keith Holmes, displaying contrasting styles, both retained their world middleweight titles within the distance Saturday before a hometown crowd at Show Case Arena.
Joppy came out firing and never relented in stopping fellow-American Ray Charles McElroy at 1:41 of the sixth round of their scheduled 12-rounder for the World Boxing Association championship.
Holmes, like Joppy a Maryland resident, fought defensively before pouring on the power late to stop British challenger Richie Woodhall in the 12th round to keep his World Boxing Council crown.
Joppy continually found the target with right hand leads as he improved his unbeaten record to 23-0-1, but McElroy was not impressed.

"He hits, but he don't hit that good," said McElroy, 21-5, who was used as a punching bag by the shorter and quicker Joppy but never hit the floor. "He hits, but he hits like a woman. Those were powder puff rights."
But when McElroy was backed up into the corner by a Joppy flurry and failed to reply, the bout was waved to a halt.
"He was tougher than I thought," admitted Joppy. "But I knew he couldn't keep taking it and I'd get him sooner or later."
The result came much later for Holmes, who was beaten to the punch and confused by the gangly Woodhall for much of the fight.
Holmes hit harder but Woodhall, a 1988 Olympic bronze medalist, was game and in great shape, dancing on his toes and flicking combinations at the southpaw until the end.
The first half of the bout was dull and defensive but from the sixth round the pace quickened. In the seventh, Holmes caught Woodhall with a right upper cut that drew blood from the Briton's nose.
Woodhall responded bravely to every combination thrown by Holmes, but the challenger packed little power in his punches and finally caved in to a determined assault by the champion.
A straight left completed a stinging combination late in the 12th and dropped Woodhall to the canvas for the first time in his professional career.
The Briton got up but was sent staggering across the ring and the fight was called 28 seconds from the final bell after he was trapped against the ropes and swarmed over by Holmes.
Holmes improved to 30-1. Woodhall suffered his first pro defeat in falling to 21-1.
The three judges had scored the fight 107-103, 107-102 and 108-102 in Holmes's favour through 11 rounds.
"He was a little awkward and very determined," said Holmes. "Like they say, these Englishmen are stubborn."
